wrapper: You are answering a Kubernetes troubleshooting knowledge question. You cannot inspect a live cluster. Given only the information below, answer concisely but precisely with four numbered parts: 1. likely diagnosis and important alternatives, 2. exact read-only kubectl commands or observations you would use to distinguish them, 3. least-risk repair options, 4. important Kubernetes caveats or edge cases. Do not invent observed output. Do not assume facts that are not stated.

tasks.prompt: A Deployment that previously ran normally is updated with a new container configuration. After the rollout, all new Pods remain Pending while the old ReplicaSet continues serving traffic. The nodes are Ready and there is no image-pull failure. The scheduler reports that none of the available nodes can accept the new Pods because of memory-related constraints. Explain what could have changed in the Pod specification, how to distinguish scheduling reservations from actual runtime memory consumption, and what repairs preserve intended workload behavior without simply hiding the problem.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies changed memory requests or placement constraints as scheduling causes and separates scheduler reservation from runtime usage. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.evidence: Checks Pod-template requests, node Allocatable and allocated resources, scheduler events, and actual usage separately. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.repair: Corrects an unjustified request or adds capacity while preserving the workload's real requirement. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.caveats: States that requests drive scheduling, limits constrain runtime, and sufficient total capacity on other nodes does not make an individual node schedulable. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]

tasks.prompt: An application receives configuration from the same ConfigMap in two ways: one value is an environment variable and another is a file inside the container. The ConfigMap is modified while the Pod runs. Several minutes later the file contains the new value, but the environment variable still contains the old value. No rollout or restart occurred. Explain why both observations can be correct, what Pod-spec variations could prevent the file from updating, how to verify the configuration path, and when a restart is necessary.

criteria.diagnosis: Distinguishes static environment-variable injection from eventually refreshed ordinary ConfigMap volumes and non-refreshing subPath mounts. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-pod-configmap.md#5a7bbfd02019b027c74341d2861906a3e72e1f88]
criteria.evidence: Checks the ConfigMap, Pod template references, mounted file, environment, and mount form. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-pod-configmap.md#5a7bbfd02019b027c74341d2861906a3e72e1f88]
criteria.repair: Uses a controlled rollout for environment or subPath consumers and a reload-capable ordinary volume for dynamic files. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-pod-configmap.md#5a7bbfd02019b027c74341d2861906a3e72e1f88]
criteria.caveats: Notes Kubelet sync and cache delay, annotation refresh, application reload behavior, and the subPath exception. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-pod-configmap.md#5a7bbfd02019b027c74341d2861906a3e72e1f88]

tasks.prompt: A normally stable application experiences a large traffic spike. One container terminates and is restarted by Kubernetes. Determine whether the process exceeded a container-level memory constraint, the node experienced memory pressure, or another mechanism caused the restart. Describe the evidence that distinguishes these cases, how requests and limits affect interpretation, and how the safest repair differs by cause.

criteria.diagnosis: Separates a container memory-limit OOM from node pressure, probe failure, and application exit. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md#40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6]
criteria.evidence: Uses container Last State and events, resource limits and requests, Pod usage, and node conditions and events. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md#40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6; content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.repair: Changes the limit or application after container OOM evidence, and addresses node capacity or placement after node-pressure evidence. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md#40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6]
criteria.caveats: States that requests are scheduling inputs rather than guarantees of actual usage, QoS is Pod-wide, and CPU throttling is not an OOM kill. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md#40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6]

tasks.prompt: A Deployment update creates a new ReplicaSet, but the rollout never completes. Some old Pods remain available, while the new ReplicaSet has fewer Ready replicas than expected. The image pulls successfully and the new containers start. Describe a diagnostic sequence using Deployment conditions, ReplicaSets, Pod status, probes, events and rollout history. Explain when rollback is appropriate and what could make rollback less reliable than expected.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies rollout progress or readiness failure and explains old/new ReplicaSet coexistence using rollout strategy. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md#2ec9ba7c01996e278991f54886d4f9fd97c2c20b]
criteria.evidence: Checks Deployment conditions, ReplicaSet counts, Pod status and events, probes, and rollout history. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md#2ec9ba7c01996e278991f54886d4f9fd97c2c20b]
criteria.repair: Uses evidence-led manifest correction or rollback to a known-good revision without manually managing ReplicaSets. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md#2ec9ba7c01996e278991f54886d4f9fd97c2c20b]
criteria.caveats: Correctly explains maxSurge, maxUnavailable, readiness, progressDeadlineSeconds, and that rollback may not help with shared external or cluster failures. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md#2ec9ba7c01996e278991f54886d4f9fd97c2c20b]

tasks.prompt: A Deployment performs a rolling update. New Pods reach Running quickly and eventually show Ready, but users experience intermittent failures. The application needs several seconds after startup before it can safely receive production requests, and shutdown needs time to drain existing work. Explain which lifecycle and rollout mechanisms to investigate, how apparently Ready or Running Pods could still contribute, and how to make the rollout safer without simply reducing availability.

criteria.diagnosis: Distinguishes startup, readiness, liveness, termination and rollout availability as separate lifecycle concerns. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md#82fb8b2984920b3ea212eeb68b5990f3955eb08e]
criteria.evidence: Checks probe definitions and events, rollout strategy, termination grace, lifecycle hooks, endpoint state, and application logs. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md#82fb8b2984920b3ea212eeb68b5990f3955eb08e]
criteria.repair: Makes readiness represent safe traffic acceptance, allows startup and drain time, and tunes rollout limits without an unjustified availability reduction. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md#82fb8b2984920b3ea212eeb68b5990f3955eb08e]
criteria.caveats: Separates Running from Ready, liveness from readiness, startup protection from steady-state checks, and termination from endpoint removal. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md#82fb8b2984920b3ea212eeb68b5990f3955eb08e]

tasks.prompt: A Pod repeatedly enters a back-off state. Each container starts, runs briefly, then exits. By inspection time, current logs contain little useful information. Describe the investigation order before changing the workload. Include how to distinguish application exit, probe-triggered restart, resource termination and configuration failure, and which evidence can disappear or change between restarts.

criteria.diagnosis: Distinguishes process exit, probe restart, resource termination, and configuration or mount failure. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-running-pod.md#287d4d6d0b86376d4ef771d105edbf5d82dba972]
criteria.evidence: Uses current and previous logs, Last State and exit code, Pod specification, describe output, and events in a safe order. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-running-pod.md#287d4d6d0b86376d4ef771d105edbf5d82dba972]
criteria.repair: Identifies the cause before changing the controller and avoids deleting evidence or disabling probes without justification. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-running-pod.md#287d4d6d0b86376d4ef771d105edbf5d82dba972]
criteria.caveats: Notes that previous logs and ephemeral filesystem state can disappear, and that a controller—not an individual Pod—is normally the repair target. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-running-pod.md#287d4d6d0b86376d4ef771d105edbf5d82dba972]

tasks.prompt: A Service has a valid ClusterIP. Three application Pods in the same namespace are Running and Ready, and each responds when contacted directly by Pod IP. Requests through the Service fail, and Kubernetes reports no usable backend addresses. Explain what Service-to-Pod relationships to verify, which endpoint-related API objects to inspect on a current Kubernetes cluster, and what configuration mistakes could produce this symptom.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies selector, readiness, port, and endpoint-publication causes and distinguishes current EndpointSlices from the deprecated Endpoints API. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-service.md#debcff5ee490b6e7b033a09f71563a5c481ff118; content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md#01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]
criteria.evidence: Checks Service selector and ports, Pod labels and readiness, all EndpointSlices for the Service, endpoint conditions, and relevant events. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md#01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]
criteria.repair: Corrects the Service or Pod template only after evidence identifies the mismatch and does not hand-edit controller-owned endpoint data. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-service.md#debcff5ee490b6e7b033a09f71563a5c481ff118]
criteria.caveats: Notes that EndpointSlices are aggregated, may be multiple, and are the current kube-proxy source of truth. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md#01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]

tasks.prompt: Pods in namespace app communicate with one another successfully. After a new NetworkPolicy is introduced, application traffic still works, but DNS lookups for Kubernetes Services time out. DNS components are healthy. Explain how to determine which traffic direction is blocked, what selectors and ports matter, the narrowest safe policy change, and why an apparently reasonable ingress rule might have no effect on DNS.

criteria.diagnosis: Explains independent ingress and egress isolation and identifies DNS as egress from the application or ingress to DNS when DNS Pods are selected. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md#22f3515ce15eb97378d7b5bf70c5a8cfab2fdb77]
criteria.evidence: Checks policy selectors, policyTypes, to/from selectors, ports, DNS Service and Pods, and policy applicability. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md#22f3515ce15eb97378d7b5bf70c5a8cfab2fdb77]
criteria.repair: Adds only the required namespace, Pod, protocol and port allow rules while retaining intended isolation. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md#22f3515ce15eb97378d7b5bf70c5a8cfab2fdb77]
criteria.caveats: States policies are additive, ingress and egress are evaluated independently, and DNS queries use the application Pod's outbound path. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md#22f3515ce15eb97378d7b5bf70c5a8cfab2fdb77]

tasks.prompt: A Pod can connect to a Service using its ClusterIP but cannot resolve the Service using its fully qualified Kubernetes DNS name. The Service exists, has healthy backends and is reachable by IP. Describe a diagnostic sequence that isolates DNS failure. Distinguish Service identity, Pod DNS configuration, cluster DNS, NetworkPolicy and namespace search behavior, and state which should and should not affect a fully qualified Service name.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies Pod DNS configuration or cluster DNS failure and correctly says a fully qualified Service name does not depend on the local namespace search list. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md#72b55df9506e88c3fb5d0b740543331b6205d85c]
criteria.evidence: Checks resolv.conf, direct DNS queries, DNS Pods and Service, policy on DNS traffic, and the exact name and namespace. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md#72b55df9506e88c3fb5d0b740543331b6205d85c]
criteria.repair: Uses targeted DNS or policy correction after evidence and does not restart CoreDNS or Pods as the first unexplained action. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md#72b55df9506e88c3fb5d0b740543331b6205d85c]
criteria.caveats: Distinguishes short-name search behavior from FQDN behavior, Service identity from DNS health, and headless records from ClusterIP routing. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md#72b55df9506e88c3fb5d0b740543331b6205d85c]

tasks.prompt: A PersistentVolumeClaim uses a valid StorageClass and remains Pending. The CSI controller is healthy, no provisioning error is visible, and sufficient storage capacity is available. The application Pod that will consume the claim has not yet been scheduled. Explain what StorageClass behavior could make this intentional, what objects and fields to inspect, and what event should cause binding or provisioning to proceed.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies WaitForFirstConsumer as intentional delayed binding and links it to consumer scheduling and topology. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.evidence: Checks PVC events, StorageClass volumeBindingMode and provisioner, consumer Pod scheduling events, and topology constraints. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.repair: Fixes the consumer's scheduling constraints or the identified provisioning issue rather than changing a valid delayed-binding class blindly. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.caveats: Explains that binding and Pod scheduling interact and that a healthy CSI controller does not imply a schedulable consumer. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]

tasks.prompt: A stateful application has used a persistent volume successfully. After the Pod is replaced, the new Pod cannot start because the volume cannot be attached or mounted. The PVC is Bound and the underlying storage resource exists. Explain causes involving scheduling location, access semantics, attachment state and stale consumers, and what to inspect before changing or deleting storage objects.

criteria.diagnosis: Considers attachment, node or zone placement, access mode and stale consumer causes for a Bound claim. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.evidence: Checks PVC/PV, Pod and node events, access modes, volume affinity, VolumeAttachment and CSI state before destructive action. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.repair: Corrects placement or attachment state and avoids deleting a bound storage object without confirmed recovery and data-safety grounds. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.caveats: Distinguishes Bound from attached or mounted, access-mode matching from enforcement, and controller identity from manual Pod deletion. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]

tasks.prompt: A new PersistentVolumeClaim uses an existing StorageClass, remains Pending, and repeated provisioning attempts fail. The API objects are syntactically valid and the cluster uses an external CSI provisioner. Describe the investigation path from PVC events through StorageClass configuration to the CSI controller and storage system. Explain which apparent fixes are risky because they bypass or conflict with dynamic provisioning.

criteria.diagnosis: Separates PVC or StorageClass validation from CSI controller and external storage failures. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.evidence: Follows PVC events to StorageClass provisioner and parameters, CSI controller status/logs, and provider-side evidence. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.repair: Repairs the identified provisioner or configuration issue and avoids manually binding a PV as a substitute for a failing dynamic workflow. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.caveats: Notes that the external provisioner and storage system are outside the API server and that deleting storage can risk data. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]

tasks.prompt: ServiceAccount client in namespace frontend must read ConfigMaps in namespace backend, with only get and list in backend and no access elsewhere or cluster-wide. Describe the RBAC objects required, where each belongs, how the ServiceAccount subject is represented, and how to verify permission before deploying the workload.

criteria.diagnosis: Defines a Role in backend and a RoleBinding in backend binding the frontend ServiceAccount, with no cluster-wide grant. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.evidence: Checks Role rules, RoleBinding namespace and subject namespace, ServiceAccount identity, and exact auth can-i results in backend and elsewhere. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.repair: Creates or corrects only the backend-scoped Role and binding with core ConfigMap get/list permissions. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.caveats: States a RoleBinding referencing a ClusterRole remains namespace-scoped, while a ClusterRoleBinding is cluster-wide, and permissions are additive. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]

tasks.prompt: A user can list and get Pods in namespace dev, but reading container logs is forbidden. The existing Role grants get and list on pods. Explain why these permissions may be insufficient, what RBAC rule to inspect or add, and how to verify effective authorization without granting broad access.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies logs as the pods/log subresource and the required get permission, separate from get/list on pods. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.evidence: Tests get pods/log with auth can-i and inspects the effective Role, binding and subject in dev. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.repair: Adds only get on pods/log in the intended namespace and does not add broad Pod or cluster permissions. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.caveats: Explains slash-delimited subresources and that wildcard resources can unintentionally include future subresources. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]

tasks.prompt: A ServiceAccount used by one application can perform operations unrelated to the Role defined in its namespace. The namespace Role looks restricted. Describe how to determine where additional permissions come from, including namespaced and cluster-scoped bindings, aggregated permissions and effective-authorization checks. Explain why inspecting only the nearest Role can mislead.

criteria.diagnosis: Traces cumulative permissions through RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings and aggregated ClusterRoles rather than only the local Role. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.evidence: Lists namespace and cluster bindings, follows roleRef and aggregation labels, and uses auth can-i as the effective check. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.repair: Removes or narrows the identified unnecessary binding at its owner while preserving required permissions. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.caveats: Distinguishes a RoleBinding to a ClusterRole from a ClusterRoleBinding, notes aggregation reconciliation, and avoids confusing Pod security context with API authorization. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md#c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]

tasks.prompt: A healthy Deployment has CPU usage from Metrics Server. An HPA with a percentage-based CPU target reports that current utilization cannot be determined and never scales. Describe what workload configuration to inspect, why raw CPU measurements may be insufficient, what HPA conditions or events confirm the diagnosis, and the safest repair.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies missing CPU requests as the likely reason percentage utilization cannot be calculated, while considering metrics API failure. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]
criteria.evidence: Checks HPA conditions and events, metric type, target Pods, every relevant CPU request, and the resource metrics API. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]
criteria.repair: Adds evidence-based requests or changes to an appropriate raw or named-container metric without hiding missing data. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]
criteria.caveats: States utilization is usage relative to requests, all relevant containers matter for Pod resource metrics, and raw usage alone is insufficient. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]

tasks.prompt: A Deployment reports the desired number of Ready replicas. The Service exists and has backend addresses, but clients receive connection failures. Do not assume a Ready Pod proves reachability through the complete Service path. Describe a layered investigation from Service configuration through endpoints, Pod ports, readiness, application listeners and NetworkPolicy, and what observations eliminate each layer.

criteria.diagnosis: Uses a layered Service path diagnosis and does not treat Ready as proof of correct port, listener, routing, or policy behavior. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-service.md#debcff5ee490b6e7b033a09f71563a5c481ff118]
criteria.evidence: Checks Service ports and selectors, EndpointSlices, Pod readiness and ports, in-Pod listener behavior, and NetworkPolicy. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-service.md#debcff5ee490b6e7b033a09f71563a5c481ff118; content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md#01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]
criteria.repair: Changes only the failing layer after a read-only observation and avoids restarting healthy workloads as the first response. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-service.md#debcff5ee490b6e7b033a09f71563a5c481ff118]
criteria.caveats: Distinguishes readiness from reachability and Service ClusterIP routing from application listener or NetworkPolicy behavior. [source: content/en/docs/tasks/debug/debug-application/debug-service.md#debcff5ee490b6e7b033a09f71563a5c481ff118]

tasks.prompt: Several unrelated Pods on one node begin failing around the same time. Some restart, another becomes Pending after replacement, and events mention resource pressure. Other nodes remain healthy. Determine whether this is primarily an application problem, node-level resource problem or scheduling consequence. Include node conditions, allocatable resources, Pod termination reasons, events and placement, and remediation only after node-level diagnosis.

criteria.diagnosis: Distinguishes a node-wide pressure incident from an application-specific failure and from a resulting scheduling failure. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3; content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md#40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6]
criteria.evidence: Checks node conditions and events, allocatable versus allocated resources, affected Pod reasons, placement and scheduler events. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.repair: Relieves confirmed node pressure or repairs the offending workload after evidence, then addresses replacement scheduling; does not apply blanket limits first. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md#40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6]
criteria.caveats: Covers memory, disk and PID pressure, QoS and eviction, requests versus usage, taints, and the fact that CPU throttling is not an OOM kill. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md#40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6]

tasks.prompt: During a Deployment rollout, a Service sometimes sends traffic to old and new Pods. Some old Pods have a deletion timestamp, and clients see connections to old replicas fail only near termination. The Service object and its selector are unchanged. The cluster has multiple backend-discovery objects for this Service. Explain how to identify the complete current backend set, determine which terminating endpoints a proxy may use, and distinguish an empty or mismatched selector from normal rollout behavior.
expected_facts: EndpointSlices are the current source of truth for kube-proxy and all slices for the Service must be aggregated; duplicate endpoints can occur during updates.
An endpoint becomes terminating after Pod deletion starts; proxies normally ignore terminating endpoints but may use serving and terminating endpoints when all available endpoints are terminating.
The Service selector and EndpointSlice service-name label or owner reference should be checked before treating rollout-time changes as a selector failure.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies EndpointSlice aggregation and distinguishes normal terminating-endpoint behavior from selector mismatch. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md@01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]
criteria.evidence: Requests inspection of all EndpointSlices for the Service, endpoint conditions, owner or service-name labels, Pod deletion timestamps, and the Service selector. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md@01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]
criteria.repair: Recommends correcting the selector or endpoint-producing controller only when evidence supports it, and otherwise uses rollout or termination configuration changes rather than manually editing controller-owned endpoints. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md@01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]
criteria.caveats: States that slices can be multiple or temporarily duplicate, ready is related to serving and termination, and terminating endpoints may be used only when all available endpoints terminate. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices.md@01d1a4747f7796d597c051a42a2d58ae88baef35]

tasks.prompt: A support group can list and get Pods and read their logs in namespace support, but it cannot start an interactive command in a running container; the API returns forbidden. No cluster-wide access is intended. Explain what authorization target and verb the command uses, where the least-privilege rule and binding should live, and how to verify the permission without broadening access.
expected_facts: Interactive container access is a Pod subresource distinct from the top-level Pod resource and must be authorized separately.
The least-privilege rule is namespaced, uses the core API group, names the exec subresource, and grants the verb needed by the exec API rather than relying on pods get or list.
A RoleBinding in support limits the permission to support, while a ClusterRoleBinding would broaden it; auth can-i should test the exact subresource request.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies the separate pods/exec subresource and the correct authorization verb for the interactive request. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md@c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.evidence: Uses an exact auth can-i check for the subresource, and inspects the Role and RoleBinding in support rather than only the top-level Pod rule. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md@c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.repair: Adds only the required subresource rule to a Role bound in support, without changing the existing Pod-read permissions or granting cluster-wide access. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md@c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]
criteria.caveats: Explains slash-delimited subresources, additive permissions, namespace scope of RoleBinding, and the risk of wildcard resources or verbs. [source: content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac.md@c269a6149f5c3ca8aa4817015e159e0aa4446ea2]

tasks.prompt: An HPA with a percentage-based CPU target scaled a Deployment correctly before a telemetry sidecar was added. After the sidecar was added, kubectl top reports CPU for both containers, but the HPA reports that utilization cannot be determined and takes no scaling action. The application container has a CPU request; the telemetry container does not. Explain the calculation, what to inspect, and how to repair this without masking load from either container.
expected_facts: Percentage CPU utilization uses current usage divided by CPU request; if a targeted Pod container lacks the relevant request, utilization for that Pod is undefined and the HPA takes no action for that metric.
Pod-level resource utilization sums containers, so a sidecar changes both usage and the request denominator; ContainerResource can target a named container when that is the intended policy.
HPA status, conditions, events, metric configuration, and every target container resource request should be inspected before changing thresholds.

criteria.diagnosis: Identifies the missing sidecar CPU request as the primary reason percentage utilization is undefined and distinguishes it from a metrics API failure. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md@c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]
criteria.evidence: Checks HPA status or conditions, metric type, target Pods, resource requests for every relevant container, and the resource metrics API. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md@c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]
criteria.repair: Adds an evidence-based CPU request to the sidecar or deliberately changes to a named ContainerResource target, preserving a meaningful denominator rather than merely lowering the target percentage. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md@c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]
criteria.caveats: Distinguishes Pod-summed utilization from named-container utilization and notes that raw metrics alone do not define percentage utilization. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md@c81548ff4915bb2af9b658e05c697e2ec0184d24]

tasks.prompt: A stateful workload has used one PVC successfully. The original Pod is terminating, and its replacement on another node remains Pending or ContainerCreating. The claim is Bound and the backend volume still exists; a second Pod from the same controller also references the claim. Explain what storage and scheduling facts to inspect, how to distinguish single-node from single-Pod access semantics, and the safest repair before changing or deleting storage objects.
expected_facts: ReadWriteOnce permits read-write mounting by one node and can allow multiple Pods on that node; ReadWriteOncePod restricts read-write mounting to one Pod across the cluster.

PVC and PV access modes are matching information, while actual attach or mount failures also require checking node or zone affinity, VolumeAttachment state, CSI events, and stale termination of the old consumer.
Deleting or recreating a bound PVC or PV is not a first repair because it can risk data loss or conflict with the controller's ownership.

criteria.diagnosis: Frames the failure as an access, placement, attachment, or stale-consumer distinction and explicitly differentiates ReadWriteOnce from ReadWriteOncePod. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md@ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.evidence: Inspects PVC and PV access modes, Pod volume references and events, node or zone placement, VolumeAttachment objects, and the previous Pod's deletion state. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md@ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.repair: Prefers waiting for or correcting the attachment and scheduling condition, or correcting the workload's access expectation, before any destructive storage operation. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md@ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]
criteria.caveats: States that RWO is node-scoped, RWOP is Pod-scoped, access modes do not generally enforce write protection after mount, and RWOP requires compatible CSI support. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md@ea0880a3f91d33553f6630a5f350330429a41cd1]

tasks.prompt: A node reports MemoryPressure=True. Pod A disappears with a kubelet termination message, while a container in Pod B reports OOMKilled; both had been running on that node. Pod A had no CPU or memory requests or limits. Pod B had equal CPU and memory requests and limits. A replacement for Pod A is now Pending. Explain the separate failure paths, what resource and placement evidence to inspect, and how the safest remediation differs.
expected_facts: A kubelet eviction caused by node pressure terminates the Pod, while OOMKilled identifies a container or cgroup memory kill; these are not interchangeable diagnoses.

Pod A is BestEffort and Pod B meets Guaranteed QoS criteria for the stated CPU and memory settings; under node pressure BestEffort is considered before Burstable and Guaranteed, with requests affecting eviction candidacy.
A replacement can remain Pending because scheduling uses node allocatable resources and current placement constraints, independently of the original termination reason.

criteria.diagnosis: Separates kubelet node-pressure eviction from container OOMKilled and correctly classifies the two stated QoS cases. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md@40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6; content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md@cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.evidence: Uses Pod termination reason and events, node conditions and events, resource requests or limits, QoS, allocatable resources, and the replacement Pod's scheduler events. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md@40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6; content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md@cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.repair: Repairs the diagnosed path separately: reduce node pressure or move workloads after evidence of eviction, adjust the offending container limit or application memory after OOM evidence, and resolve scheduling constraints for the replacement. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md@40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6; content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md@cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]
criteria.caveats: Notes that requests are not actual usage, CPU limits cause throttling rather than an OOM kill, QoS is derived across containers, and eviction can terminate all containers in a Pod. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos.md@40102b8a1bf4c97f6d7f6834c9636756c87daaf6; content/en/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md@cbd80b3d4d61f92226570516bac9f94ceb9155a3]

tasks.prompt: A Service object named payments exists in namespace prod. It has no ClusterIP and no selector. Resolving payments.prod.svc.cluster.local returns a CNAME for payments.vendor.example. Connections work when the vendor hostname is used directly, but HTTPS requests using the in-cluster Service name fail hostname or certificate checks. Explain what the object is doing, what to inspect, and the safest client or Service change.
expected_facts: A Service without a ClusterIP or selector that returns a CNAME is a DNS mapping to an external name, not a proxy or virtual-IP backend.
No packet forwarding or endpoint load balancing is provided; clients reach the external hostname after DNS resolution.
The in-cluster hostname differs from the external hostname, so HTTP Host headers or TLS certificate name validation can fail; use the correct hostname or redesign the Service/client boundary.

criteria.diagnosis: Infers the DNS-only external Service behavior from the lack of ClusterIP or selector and the CNAME result, without treating it as a missing backend list. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/service.md@6687659207aa5a8fc2c46a86a04e0393db14a8f6]
criteria.evidence: Checks Service type and externalName, DNS records, and client protocol behavior rather than looking for Pod selectors or kube-proxy endpoints. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/service.md@6687659207aa5a8fc2c46a86a04e0393db14a8f6]
criteria.repair: Uses the externally valid hostname for protocol clients or replaces the DNS-only mapping with an appropriate in-cluster or explicitly managed endpoint design when proxying is required. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/service.md@6687659207aa5a8fc2c46a86a04e0393db14a8f6]
criteria.caveats: States that ExternalName has no proxying, hostname-sensitive HTTP and TLS protocols can fail, and an IPv4-looking externalName is treated as a DNS name rather than an IP address. [source: content/en/docs/concepts/services-networking/service.md@6687659207aa5a8fc2c46a86a04e0393db14a8f6]
